1.title: Taxonomy of Blockchain Technologies. Principles of Identification and Classification

2.title: Crypto-asset Taxonomy for Investors and Regulators

term_types.name: Consensus Network Topology
term_types.question: How are nodes interconnected and how does information flow for transaction validation?
term_types.description: Describes the type of interconnection between nodes and the information flow used for transaction validation.

values.definition: Peer-to-peer network where every node is equivalent and validates transactions independently.
Network where nodes have differentiated roles, such as tracking and validating nodes, also called consortium blockchains.
Network where a central authority controls what is added to the ledger.

citations.quote: Consensus Network Topology describes the type of interconnection between the nodes and the type of information flow between them for transaction and/or for the purpose of validation.

term_types.name: Consensus Immutability and Failure Tolerance
term_types.question: What mechanism ensures immutability and tolerance to failures of the agreed ledger?
term_types.description: Defines the mechanism that keeps the ledger reliable, valid and secure against faults and malicious behaviour.

values.definition: Miners solve cryptographic hash puzzles to create blocks, with probability proportional to computing power devoted.
Block creation probability depends on share of digital assets held, with randomised or coin-age-based selection.
Only pre-selected trusted authority nodes are allowed to create new blocks and secure the blockchain.
Provers allocate hard-drive or storage space instead of CPU cycles to compete for block creation.
Miners prove they burned digital assets by sending them to unspendable addresses.
Combines mechanisms such as PoB with PoS, or PoW with PoS, where one acts as checkpoints for the other.

citations.quote: As of this writing, we identify six main layouts for Consensus Immutability and Failure Tolerance

term_types.name: Gossiping
term_types.question: How does information propagate through the peer network?
term_types.description: Describes how new blocks and information travel across nodes in the network.

values.definition: Information first spreads locally through a federated validation process before reaching all nodes.
Information is sent to a randomly selected list of peers in a largely unstructured network topology.

citations.quote: We identify two possible layouts for Gossiping: 1. Local. Gossiping occurs first in a local manner (through a local validation process) until consensus is reached.

term_types.name: Latency
term_types.question: What rule governs message propagation timing in the network?
term_types.description: Sub-subcomponent describing whether message delays are bounded in the consensus agreement.

values.definition: Systems set upper bounds on process speed and communication delay, discarding messages exceeding the interval.
No bound is set on process speed or communication delay; messages may take indefinite time to arrive.

citations.quote: Systems which set upper bounds on process speed interval and communication delay such that every message arrives within a certain known, predefined, time interval are called synchronous.

term_types.name: Finality
term_types.question: Can recorded information be considered perpetually stored once recorded?
term_types.description: Sub-subcomponent describing whether consensus converges deterministically or only probabilistically.

values.definition: Consensus eventually settles probabilistically; previously validated blocks may still be pruned later.
Consensus converges with certainty and transactions are immediately confirmed or rejected.

citations.quote: We identify two possible layouts for Finality: 1. Non-Deterministic. In this case, consensus agreement eventually settles.

term_types.name: Data Structure in the Blockheader
term_types.question: Which tree structure is used to store transaction information in the block header?
term_types.description: Describes the capability of the system to store transaction information in block headers.

values.definition: Block header stores a root hash of a binary Merkle tree containing that block's transactions.
Tree storing transactions, receipts and state, allowing verification of specific branches and account updates.

citations.quote: We identify two possible layouts for Data Structure in the blockheader: 1. Binary Merkle Tree. Bitcoin uses the Binary Merkle tree within the block header to store the transactions.

term_types.name: Transaction Model
term_types.question: How are user information and transaction inputs and outputs recorded and updated in the ledger?
term_types.description: Describes how nodes store and update user information in the distributed ledger.

values.definition: Outputs are locked for a number of blocks before reuse, preventing spending of unstable fees and rewards.
Transactions recorded as balance increments and decrements in an account-style ledger.

citations.quote: The transaction model can be imagined as an accounting ledger which tracks the inputs and outputs of each transaction.

term_types.name: Server Storage
term_types.question: Which nodes store the full blockchain versus a subset of it?
term_types.description: Describes whether nodes hold the complete ledger or only selected information.

values.definition: All nodes hold the full information of the blockchain, creating redundancy and resilience.
Some nodes store only a selected subset of blockchain information, improving scalability but reducing resiliency.

citations.quote: We identify two possible layouts for Server Storage: 1. Full Nodes. All nodes connected to the network, and which are part of the validation process, are of the same kind.

term_types.name: Block Storage
term_types.question: What information is stored in the blockchain?
term_types.description: Determines which information is stored on-chain, affecting scalability and abstraction of user data.

values.definition: Only transactions with inputs and outputs are stored, as in Bitcoin or IOTA's directed acyclic graph.
Decentralised storage also records user balances in specific assets, as in Ripple.

citations.quote: We identify two possible layouts for Block Storage: 1. Transactions. In systems like Bitcoin, only the transactions are stored.

term_types.name: Limits to Scalability
term_types.question: Which factor most limits how the system scales as its size grows?
term_types.description: Identifies the most limiting element for scaling the system (transactions, users, nodes, or confirmation time).

values.definition: Throughput is capped by design, such as a hard-coded block size limit in Bitcoin.
Scalability is constrained by the number of objects or accounts whose states are stored, as in Ripple or Ethereum.
Gossip propagation time across many nodes limits consensus and may cause forks.
Scaling is constrained by how long it takes actions to be added and validated in blocks, deterministic or stochastic.

citations.quote: We identify four possible layouts as Limits to Scalability: 1. Limit by number of transactions. We start from the most common real-world example.

term_types.name: Native Asset
term_types.question: Does the system have an underlying native currency, and can it convert other assets?
term_types.description: Describes whether the system has a native digital asset and whether it supports multiple convertible assets.

values.definition: Private implementations do not require a native asset to incentivise participation.
Only the platform's own token can be transferred, such as Bitcoin or Litecoin.
Platform supports exchange of assets expressed in currencies outside those native to the platform.

citations.quote: We identify three possible layouts for Native asset: 1. None. Private blockchain implementations do not require a native asset within to incentivise participation.

term_types.name: Tokenisation
term_types.question: Can tokens representing ownership be created on the platform?
term_types.description: Describes whether and how the platform supports issuing tokens that represent property ownership.

values.definition: Platform has no technology enabling tokenisation without third-party additions.
Tokenised transactions enabled on the base chain via add-ons such as Colored Coins.
Native tokenisation via smart contracts, as in Ethereum, enabling creation of arbitrary new tokens.

citations.quote: We identify three possible layouts for Tokenisation: 1. No tokenisation present. Without third-party technologies, Bitcoin does not have implemented technologies that enable tokenisation.

term_types.name: Asset Supply Management
term_types.question: How is the supply of the digital asset created and limited?
term_types.description: Describes the monetary policy governing creation of the digital asset.

values.definition: Supply grows sub-linearly toward a well-defined maximum, as introduced in Bitcoin.
Supply has no defined maximum limit, as in Dogecoin or Freicoin.
All assets distributed before system start, with a reward system inducing later redistribution.

citations.quote: We identify three possible layouts for Asset Supply Management: 1. Limited - Deterministic. The most replicated system in the world of blockchain is the limited supply.

term_types.name: Interoperability
term_types.question: Can the blockchain exchange information with systems outside blockchains?
term_types.description: Describes the capability to exchange information with external, non-blockchain systems.

values.definition: Turing-complete script language allows conditions referencing external system status via APIs.
Non-Turing-complete language or built-in tools purposely enable interaction with the real world.
Blockchain has no means to interact with other systems outside it.

citations.quote: We identify three possible layouts for Interoperability: 1. Implicit interoperability. It occurs when the smart contracts that specify conditions can be written in a Turing-complete blockchain script language.

term_types.name: Intraoperability
term_types.question: Can the blockchain exchange information with other blockchains?
term_types.description: Describes the capability to exchange information between different blockchains.

values.definition: Turing-complete script language allows conditions referencing status on other blockchains.
Non-Turing-complete language specifically designed to allow intraoperability, such as Bitcoin with Counterparty.
Blockchain cannot interact with other blockchains without external solutions.

citations.quote: Intraoperability illustrates the overall capability of blockchains to exchange information with other blockchains.

term_types.name: Governance
term_types.question: Who defines and maintains the technical rules of the blockchain?
term_types.description: Describes the model by which technical rules and upgrades are determined.

values.definition: Open communities of developers and validators coordinate upgrades and technical adjustments.
Enterprises with technical strength dictate technical rules according to their business goals.
Industry consortia of companies with common business demands set technical rules collectively.

citations.quote: We identify two type of governance rules: 1) technical rules of self-governance defined by the participants.

term_types.name: Script Language
term_types.question: How expressive is the scripting language used to define conditions and smart contracts?
term_types.description: Describes the expressiveness and computational scope of the scripting language.

values.definition: Language can execute arbitrary algorithmic computations, as in the Ethereum Virtual Machine.
Limited-scope language chosen to keep computation impact low, as in Bitcoin.
Non-Turing-complete language purposely designed for specific cases, such as DAML for financial rights.
Non-Turing-complete language that uses trusted oracles to incorporate external data.

citations.quote: We identify four possible layouts for Script Language: 1. Turing Complete. Ethereum refers to a suite of protocols that define a platform for decentralised applications.

term_types.name: Data Encryption
term_types.question: Which cryptographic primitive ensures authenticity, integrity and order of events?
term_types.description: Describes the cryptographic primitives used for authenticity and integrity.

values.definition: Secure Hash Algorithm family (SHA-256, SHA-512) used for hashing transactions and integrity.
Zero-knowledge succinct non-interactive argument allowing validation without providing the underlying data.

citations.quote: We identify two major layouts for Data Encryption: 1. SHA-2. SHA stands for Secure Hash Algorithm.

term_types.name: Data Privacy
term_types.question: Is privacy built into the protocol or added externally?
term_types.description: Describes whether transaction data is obfuscated by default or through add-on solutions.

values.definition: Privacy provided by default in the protocol, such as ZeroCash, Enigma or CORDA.
Pseudonymous or public blockchains rely on external mixing, secret sharing, ring signatures or stealth addresses.

citations.quote: According to the solutions proposes so far to enhance Data Privacy, we identify two possible layouts: 1. Built-in data privacy.

term_types.name: Coding Language
term_types.question: In which programming language or languages is the codebase written?
term_types.description: Describes the interconnectivity of programming languages used in the blockchain codebase.

values.definition: Codebase is written in one programming language, such as C++ for Bitcoin Core.
Codebase and SDKs use several programming languages, such as C++, Go and JavaScript.

citations.quote: We identify two possible layouts for Coding Language: 1. Single Language. Bitcoin has released The Bitcoin Core version 0.13.1 with the underlying coding language C++.

term_types.name: Code License
term_types.question: Is the source code openly available for modification?
term_types.description: Describes whether the source code is open to modification and forking.

values.definition: Source code is publicly available under permissive licences such as MIT or ISC.
Source code is not openly distributed, typically for private implementations.

citations.quote: We identify thee possible layouts for Code License: 1. Open Source. Regardless of the exact licence used for specific projects, we refer only to the openness in the source code.

term_types.name: Software Architecture
term_types.question: Is the blockchain built as a single integrated application or as decoupled modules?
term_types.description: Describes the high-level structure of the blockchain software.

values.definition: All ledger functions are handled by a single-tier application without modularity, as in Bitcoin and Ethereum.
Consensus engine and P2P layers are decoupled from application state, as in Tendermint or Hyperledger Fabric.

citations.quote: We identify two possible layouts for Software Architecture: 1. Monolithic Design. In this case, all the aspects of a decentralised ledger are handled by a blockchain built as a single-tier software application.

term_types.name: Access and Control Layer
term_types.question: Who has read, write and consensus-management rights on the ledger?
term_types.description: Defines the authorisation and control policy determining who can read, write and manage consensus.

values.definition: All participants have read/write access and can contribute to ledger updates without control.
Read access is open to all, but write and consensus management require permission from pre-selected nodes.
Read, write and consensus rights are granted only by a centralised organisation.

citations.quote: Although different variations are possible, the authority to perform transactions on a blockchain generally belongs to one of the following main models of the Access and control Layer.

term_types.name: Identity Layer
term_types.question: Does the system verify user identities through KYC/AML procedures or allow anonymity?
term_types.description: Describes the onboarding and identification approach for entities joining the network.

values.definition: Compliant blockchain validates organisations and attribute data from authoritative sources, e.g. Stellar and Ripple.
No identity layer identifies users; pseudonymous addresses are used, as in Bitcoin.

citations.quote: We identify two possible layouts: 1. KYC/AML. Compliant blockchains have the ability to validate organisations and their attribute data from authoritative sources.

term_types.name: Reward System
term_types.question: How are participants compensated for storage, validation or verification?
term_types.description: Describes the automatic rewarding mechanisms that compensate active members.

values.definition: Fixed or variable reward to the block creator, such as the coinbase transaction in Bitcoin.
Reward for block creation plus reward for including valid forked blocks to incentivise cross-validation, as in Ethereum.

citations.quote: We identify two possible layouts for Reward System: 1. Lump-sum Reward. Individuals taking part of the storage, validation or verification process may be rewarded for their action.

term_types.name: Fee Reward
term_types.question: Are transaction fees optional, mandatory or absent?
term_types.description: Describes the nature of fees users must contribute when using the blockchain.

values.definition: Users may pay a voluntary fee that prioritises processing, as in Bitcoin.
All transactions must include fees, as required in Stellar.
No transaction fees are charged, as in Hyperledger Fabric.

citations.quote: We identify three possible layouts for Fees Reward: 1. Optional Fees. In Bitcoin and related technologies users can optionally pay a voluntary fee for the validation process.

term_types.name: Fee Structure
term_types.question: Is the fee linked to the size of the request or fixed per request?
term_types.description: Describes whether fees follow a variable or fixed structure.

values.definition: Fee depends on transaction size, paid per byte, as in Bitcoin.
Fee is linked to the request rather than its size, as in Enigma or Peercoin.

citations.quote: When provided by the system, fees can follow either a fixed or a variable structure. There are two alternative layouts for Fees Structure: 1. Variable Fees.

term_types.name: Technical Standard
term_types.question: Which technical template defines how the crypto-asset is issued and transferred across blockchains?
term_types.description: Classifies the token standard or native protocol on which the asset is built.

values.definition: Assets built on their own chain and governed by its own protocol rules rather than a smart-contract token standard.
Fungible, widely used standard enabling broad DeFi integration and wider contagion surface.
Other standards such as ERC-721 or ERC-1400/ERC-3643 used across blockchains.

citations.section: Sections 1-5: motivation, related work, methodology, taxonomy dimensions, dataclass and decision rules, mapping results (summary)
citations.quote: Native: Assets built on their own chain and governed by its own protocol rules rather than a smart-contract token standard.

term_types.name: Centralisation Dimension
term_types.question: Is governance, minting, yield and redemption control concentrated in a single entity or distributed across the network?
term_types.description: Classifies the degree of centralisation of critical resources using the Minimum Decentralisation Test across functional sub-dimensions.

values.definition: Governance, minting or redemption controlled by a single entity or tightly-layered group; token-holder influence limited.
Governance, issuance, redemption and yield broadly distributed; no single entity exercises unilateral control.
Mixed or transitional models where some domains are decentralised and others remain centrally controlled.

citations.section: Sections 1-5: motivation, related work, methodology, taxonomy dimensions, dataclass and decision rules, mapping results (summary)
citations.quote: an asset is classified as decentralised if all groups pass the MDT, centralised if the first 4 groups are subject to unilateral control by a single entity, and hybrid otherwise

term_types.name: Asset Function
term_types.question: What is the primary economic function of the crypto-asset?
term_types.description: Distinguishes assets by their economic function, such as governance, utility or exposure to underlying cash flows.

values.definition: Assets conveying on-chain governance or control rights over a protocol or pool, such as voting on parameters or upgrades.
Assets providing digital access to a specific application, good or service without claims on reserves or cash flows.
Assets whose core economic function is providing exposure to underlying assets or cash flows, behaving like securities.

citations.section: Sections 1-5: motivation, related work, methodology, taxonomy dimensions, dataclass and decision rules, mapping results (summary)
citations.quote: Security tokens: Assets whose core economic function is to provide exposure to underlying assets or cash flows, and that therefore behave similarly to traditional securities

term_types.name: Issuer
term_types.question: Who, if anyone, creates and makes commitments regarding the token?
term_types.description: Identifies whether an issuer exists and whether it is a centralised entity, protocol or none.

values.definition: Assets minted by a clearly identifiable legal person or entity that controls issuance and may promise returns or redemption.
Assets minted or distributed algorithmically via smart contracts without a single accountable party post-deployment.
Assets minted from consensus mechanisms without any centralised or delegated issuance process.

citations.section: Sections 1-5: motivation, related work, methodology, taxonomy dimensions, dataclass and decision rules, mapping results (summary)
citations.quote: No issuer: Assets minted from consensus mechanisms, without any centralised or delegated issuance process (e.g., BTC, XMR).

term_types.name: Minting Mechanism
term_types.question: How are new units of the crypto-asset created and released into circulation?
term_types.description: Classifies the process by which units originate, such as consensus, lock-and-mint, staking or wrapping.

values.definition: Units created via proof of work, proof of stake, proof of authority, proof of capacity or proof of burn.
Assets minted by depositing collateral into a contract or custodian.
Minted by staking PoS tokens to generate staking rewards.
Original asset locked on its own blockchain with a copy minted on another to enable cross-chain use.
Tokens with elastic supply adjusted to maintain a peg.
Protocol-engineered emissions as incentives or to bootstrap participation.
Assets minted at launch and distributed to founders or early buyers.
Token contracts maintaining a registry of unique ownership under non-fungible standards.

citations.section: Sections 1-5: motivation, related work, methodology, taxonomy dimensions, dataclass and decision rules, mapping results (summary)
citations.quote: Crypto-assets can be created through a variety of minting processes, which differ in their economic logic and technical implementation.

term_types.name: Yield Source
term_types.question: From which underlying economic activity or protocol emission does the holder's yield derive?
term_types.description: Distinguishes direct yield from underlying economic activity and incentive yield from protocol-engineered emissions, or no yield.

values.definition: Interest generated from borrowers in lending protocols accruing to depositors.
Trading fees rewarded to liquidity providers from automated market maker protocols.
Validator rewards distributed on proof-of-stake chains and liquid staking tokens.
Collected protocol revenues redistributed to token stakers.
Minted and distributed governance tokens to motivate protocol participants.
Value redistributed after supply adjustment in algorithmic stablecoins.
Assets that generate no yield, functioning only as stores of value or means of payment.

citations.section: Sections 1-5: motivation, related work, methodology, taxonomy dimensions, dataclass and decision rules, mapping results (summary)
citations.quote: We distinguish yield by underlying economic activity (direct yield) or by protocol-engineered emissions (incentive yield).

term_types.name: Distribution Mechanism
term_types.question: How is yield operationalised and reflected in token-holder value?
term_types.description: Defines how yield is delivered to holders, through balance changes, redemption ratio changes, price, or external rewards.

values.definition: Yield distributed by periodically adjusting the holder's balance upward.
Token quantity constant while its redemption or reference ratio to the underlying increases over time.
Neither balance nor redemption rate changes; yield distributed through price adjustment.
Yield distributed in another asset or via a distinct rewards pool.

citations.section: Sections 1-5: motivation, related work, methodology, taxonomy dimensions, dataclass and decision rules, mapping results (summary)
citations.quote: Quantity-accrual (rebasing): Yield is distributed by periodically adjusting the holder's balance upward (e.g., stETH, AMPL).

term_types.name: Reference Asset
term_types.question: Which asset, if any, is the redemption or stability reference for the crypto-asset?
term_types.description: Classifies whether the asset references fiat, other assets, or nothing, and whether it is a stablecoin.

values.definition: Stablecoins referencing a single official currency, such as MiCAR e-money tokens.
Assets purporting to maintain stable value by referencing one or more assets, defended through redemption or collateral.
Crypto-referenced tokens not intended to stabilise their own value, such as wrapped tokens and LSTs.
Assets providing no redemption right to a reference asset.

citations.section: Sections 1-5: motivation, related work, methodology, taxonomy dimensions, dataclass and decision rules, mapping results (summary)
citations.quote: ARTs: assets that purport to maintain a stable value by referencing one or more assets, and designed to defend value parity through issuer redemption or collateral mechanisms.

term_types.name: Redemption Mechanism
term_types.question: How does a holder convert the token into its reference asset?
term_types.description: Describes the operational route through which redemption is executed and where control resides.

values.definition: Issuer or custodian redeems off-chain after unilateral authorisation.
Holder repays or burns and withdraws collateral from protocol custody, enforced by smart contract.
Burn or lock a wrapped asset to release the underlying on another chain via a custodian.
Holder exits by swapping to others rather than redeeming with the issuer.
Redemption subject to queues or withdrawal windows pre-established in the protocol.
Built-in facility to swap at or near par using protocol reserves or troves.
Burn position token to withdraw a pro-rata share of pool reserves.

citations.section: Sections 1-5: motivation, related work, methodology, taxonomy dimensions, dataclass and decision rules, mapping results (summary)
citations.quote: Redemption mechanism: Assets can be further distinguished by how redemption is operationalised within the protocol.

term_types.name: Legal Classification
term_types.question: How is the crypto-asset positioned under current US and EU legal frameworks?
term_types.description: Labels whether the asset is a security or financial instrument, stable-value token, fund/AIF-type, or other crypto-asset.

values.definition: Assets meeting at least one of the US Howey test or EU MiFID financial-instrument test.
Assets failing Howey and MiFID tests but passing the MiCAR stablecoin test.
Assets satisfying Howey and triggering EU AIF classification as units or shares in a collective investment undertaking.
Assets qualifying none of the above classifications; legal claims weak or absent.

citations.section: Sections 1-5: motivation, related work, methodology, taxonomy dimensions, dataclass and decision rules, mapping results (summary)
citations.quote: With these tests, we categorize assets to 4 main categories: Security or financial instrument; Stable-value token (ART/EMT); Fund / AIF-type; Other crypto-assets or commodities.

term_types.name: Form of Claim
term_types.question: What economic rights does the holder have, along the axes of in personam versus in rem, claim target, and direction of proceeds?
term_types.description: Distinguishes the contractual or property-type nature of holder rights and where proceeds are directed.

values.value: In personam, against issuer, proceeds to issuer
values.definition: Contractual or statutory claim against the issuer, with issuer keeping the interest margin.

values.value: In personam, against issuer, proceeds to holders
values.definition: Holders have equity or profit-sharing claims on the issuing entity.

values.value: In personam, against reserve, proceeds to issuer
values.definition: Contractual claim linked to a segregated reserve pool, with issuer capturing interest margin.

values.value: In personam, against reserve, proceeds to holders
values.definition: Contractual claims on the reserve pool's cash flows allocated to tranche holders.

values.value: In rem, against reserve, proceeds to issuer
values.definition: Asset represents co-ownership or beneficial interest in a defined asset pool, with net income to investors.
Assets conferring no economic claim.

citations.section: Sections 1-5: motivation, related work, methodology, taxonomy dimensions, dataclass and decision rules, mapping results (summary)
citations.quote: we distinguish the form of rights along three orthogonal axes: (i) whether the holder has an in personam (contractual) or in rem (property-type) position, (ii) whether the claim is directed primarily against the issuer's balance sheet or against a specified reserve or asset pool, (iii) whether the proceeds are retailed by holders or by issuers

term_types.name: TradFi Analogy
term_types.question: Which traditional finance instrument category is the crypto-asset most analogous to, given its feature combination?
term_types.description: Maps combinations of features to mutually exclusive traditional finance analogues for interpretability.

values.definition: Assets minted on consensus or at genesis, analogous to commodities such as BTC or XRP.
Governance tokens analogous to voting equity shares such as UNI.
Yield-generating assets with no reference asset, distributed by increasing holder balance.
Assets minted by locking collateral and redeemed at par by protocol, analogous to repurchase agreements.
Reference-asset tokens without yield, analogous to depositary receipts such as WBTC.
Yield retained to increase redemption ratio, analogous to capitalising share classes such as cbETH.
Yield distributed by increasing holder balance with queued redemption, analogous to PTCs such as stETH.
Default when no defined analogy is found.

citations.section: Sections 1-5: motivation, related work, methodology, taxonomy dimensions, dataclass and decision rules, mapping results (summary)
citations.quote: we derive TradFi analogies (to commodities, voting equity shares, payment in kind, repo, depositary receipts, capitalising share class, and pass-through certificates (PTCs)) for matching combinations of features.
